speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: asked the Minister for Transport in enhancing road safety, what other measures can the Ministry consider besides licensing cyclists.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: asked the Minister for Transport given that cyclists are more vulnerable on the roads, how can it be ensured that (i) cyclists are protected against inconsiderate and reckless drivers and (ii) the rights of both cyclists and motor vehicle drivers are deconflicted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Speaker, may I have your permission to answer Question Nos 3 and 4 together?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is a good development, as cycling is a convenient, environmentally friendly and healthy way to travel.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The key is to ensure safety – safety for different groups of road users.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: However, it is not always possible to have separate paths for motor vehicles and bicycles.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There will be many instances and locations where motorists and cyclists have to share the same road space.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: To enhance road safety, it is important to have clear rules for motorists and cyclists, and for everyone to follow these safety rules.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For on-road cyclists, there are existing rules under the Road Traffic Act which they must follow.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For example, cyclists must comply with all traffic rules, such as adhering to traffic light signals and avoiding the use of expressways and tunnels.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They should also ride as near as possible to the far-left edge of the road.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This means they should keep to the left on the leftmost lane unless they are turning right or making a U-turn.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: On single-lane roads, cyclists are required to ride in a single file, so they do not obstruct passing vehicles.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The majority of cyclists follow the safety rules.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But there is a minority of errant cyclists who use their mobile phones while riding, refuse to stop at red lights, ride in the middle lane of a major road, including expressways where bicycles are prohibited, and some of them react aggressively when they are called out for their actions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There are also motorists who drive recklessly and endanger the lives of others, including cyclists, and we will take enforcement actions against them too.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We should bear in mind that cyclists are more vulnerable than those travelling in motor vehicles.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Active Mobility Advisory Panel (AMAP) will review ways to raise awareness amongst motorists on how to share road space safely with cyclists and other users.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Ultimately, there needs to be more graciousness, consideration, as well as give and take on the roads.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Other countries have done it and I believe so can we.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Beyond enforcement, the more enduring solution is public education.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In his written Parliamentary Question, Mr Dennis Tan asked if we have a public education campaign on safe practices for cyclists and pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Since 2018, LTA has offered the Safe Riding Programme (SRP).

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is a voluntary education programme that is free of charge, with both theory and practical components for all active mobility device users, including cyclists.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: LTA is revamping the SRP and will work with Traffic Police to reach out to road users and encourage public participation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We intend to roll out the new SRP in the next few months.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: On whether to license on-road cyclists, there are mixed views from the public.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Some are in support of licensing, so that errant cyclists can be more easily identified and punished.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Others have expressed concerns that licensing on-road cyclists will increase compliance costs and affect the livelihoods of Singaporeans who are using their bicycles for work and commute.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: AMAP will adopt a fair and balanced approach in doing its review by consulting widely and hearing from different groups of stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Most jurisdictions, like the Netherlands and Denmark, do not license cyclists.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Vienna licenses children aged 10 to 12 who ride alone on roads, to ensure they are educated with road traffic rules, but adult cyclists are not required to have a licence.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Tokyo requires bicycles to be registered, but the purpose is to deter bicycle theft and not to enhance road safety.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Beijing used to register bicycles too, but decided to abolish the scheme in 2004 as they found it to be costly and ineffective.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: AMAP will review the practices in overseas jurisdictions and study the different options and trade-offs carefully before finalising its recommendations.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Beyond reviewing the safety rules and penalties, I urge all road users to drive and ride safely, be considerate to one another and, in doing so, make our roads safer for everyone.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is good to know that MOT does not intend to license cyclists.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I have one supplementary question on enhancing safe cycling in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: PCN and cycling paths across the whole of Singapore will take time to build.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Can LTA embark on selective improvements to infrastructure that can enhance safety?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: For instance, widening of existing shared paths that are already too narrow and also adding more signages and markings on roadways, especially at road stretches with typically higher cyclist traffic and also junctions with blind spots.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is studying carefully the different options and trade-offs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: What I shared earlier in my main reply was to highlight some of the practices in overseas jurisdictions where they do not license cyclists or bicycles, but they have other ways of improving road safety.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, we do need to look at these carefully.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I believe where Ms Poh and some members of the public are coming from is that licensing may seem like an attractive idea to improve road safety, but, in practice, and based on the experiences in other countries, whether that is, indeed, an effective way or are there other more effective ways, that is something AMAP is carefully studying.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And in doing so, as Ms Poh pointed out, there will be more space for different groups of road users: pedestrians, cyclists.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is an important effort that must be complemented by users putting safety as a priority.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The footpaths may be wider, but you must still ride safely and you must still look out for bicycles, other devices and other pedestrians when you are walking along these footpaths.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: At the end of the day, I think what is most important is a combination of good infrastructure but also safety consciousness, placing priority on safety for all users.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The most important was on public education and I totally agree with the importance of public education.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Would the Ministry consider conducting safety lessons in schools?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That is one of the early touchpoints where we can educate our children.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But most importantly, in that context, would the Ministry consider working closely with MOE to inculcate this, put it into the curriculum so that our students are given better ideas of safety and road safety in the future?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But I just wanted to highlight that, currently, Primary school students do go through activities to teach them about road safety.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There is also a collaboration with Traffic Police and LTA to bring our students to the Road Safety Park and to expose them to different aspects of road safety.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is something which we can find other ways of raising awareness, not just with students but also with other groups of road users.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: LTA is working on this with Traffic Police and I hope that when the revised programme is ready, we can encourage the public to participate in this.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I wanted to find out whether it is possible for the deployment of Auxiliary Police officers to help educate cyclists and motorists at this moment and pending the review and improvements to the infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have noticed that in certain areas where cyclists like to go to, they normally cycle in a group and occupy the entire left lane.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is causing danger to themselves and also to motorists on the roads.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Often, I find there are arguments as to who has the right to the lane.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I agree with my colleagues who spoke earlier; I think education is key.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And so, pending the review, is it possible for LTA to look at public education and enforcement, to make sure all cyclists keep in one single row —

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: And just to keep to the extreme left lane.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Gan may be aware that we have been enforcing adherence to safety rules.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And this is a joint effort by Traffic Police and LTA.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We do need to recognise as well that when cyclists are on the road, they are more vulnerable compared to those who are travelling in motor vehicles.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There are some on-going discussions with different groups of stakeholders on whether this is a good practice or not.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: From one perspective, it does help to enhance safety for the cyclists.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think some cyclists also agree that the group should not be too big, but they say if they are riding in a reasonably sized group, the cars that are driving past, treat this group as though they are one slow moving vehicle.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: You pay more attention to looking out for them, being more aware of their presence on the road.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And I think they would consult widely with different groups of stakeholders before coming to the final recommendation.
